summary: Provides a profile of IKE and PKIX for using public key infrastructure with IKE/IPsec, defining requirements for certificates in this context. It complements IKEv1 and IKEv2, which assume PKI exists. It is a standards-track document.

plainLanguage.summary: Digital ID cards need rules for use in secure connections. This note says which ID details are required.

questions: how to use certificates with ipsec
what is the ipsec pki profile
what is an empty certreq in ike
which certificate extensions does ike support
subtitle: Pins down how IKE and IPsec should use X.509 certificates, so that implementations make the same choices and interoperate.

tldr.problem: IKE and the PKIX certificate profile leave many choices open for IPsec, so implementations made different choices and interoperability suffered.
tldr.mechanism: RFC 4945 profiles IKEv1/ISAKMP, IKEv2 and PKIX: it says how the ID, certificate request and certificate payloads must carry and match certificate data, which certificate extensions to use or avoid, and how revocation is handled.
tldr.outcome: Peers get agreed rules for tying an IKE identity to a certificate and to policy. Revocation data is obtained out of band rather than inside IKE.

today: RFC 4945 is a Proposed Standard published in August 2007. The unit metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it.

sections.title: Why a Profile Is Needed
sections.content:
IKE, ISAKMP and IKEv2 provide key exchange for IPsec, and peers often authenticate with digital certificates as specified in PKIX. The RFC says the combination leads to an underspecified set of requirements. ISAKMP names the contents of messages without giving their syntax or meaning, while the PKIX profile offers many mechanisms with little IPsec-specific guidance.

RFC 4945 therefore profiles both. It documents the contents and meaning of the relevant IKE payloads and narrows the PKIX framework for IKE and IPsec. It also folds in lessons from implementation and deployment experience. Material from ISAKMP, IKEv1 (RFC 2409), IKEv2 (RFC 4306) and PKIX is not repeated, and readers are assumed to know those documents.
sections.plainLanguage: If everyone fills in the same form in a different way, nobody understands anybody. This document says how to fill in the form.

sections.title: Identities and the ID Payload
sections.content:
The ID payload says who the sender claims to be. The recipient can use it as a lookup key for policy and for the peer's certificate. Implementations SHOULD fill it with identity information from the end-entity certificate, and MUST verify that the ID matches keying material the peer demonstrably holds, otherwise an inappropriate or insecure policy may be used.

Each ID type maps to a certificate field. IP addresses, FQDNs and user FQDNs must match the iPAddress, dNSName and rfc822Name entries of the SubjectAltName extension. A Distinguished Name must be the entire certificate Subject, compared bitwise. IP ranges, general names (ID_DER_ASN1_GN) and key IDs MUST NOT be sent.

  • IP addresses: implementations SHOULD NOT use them as ID, because of problems such as NAT traversal. If one is used, a mismatch with the certificate or with the packet's source address MUST abort the security association setup, unless a configuration option, off by default, skips the check.
  • FQDN and user FQDN: compared case-insensitively, with no substring or wildcard matching. Implementations SHOULD NOT use DNS to turn the name into an address for policy decisions unless the mapping is secure, for example with DNSSEC.
  • Distinguished Names: implementations MUST be able to match policy on any combination of the C, CN, O and OU attributes, and MUST NOT populate ID from an empty Subject.

A FQDN meant as an identity MUST be in the dNSName field, never only in the Subject. The sender picks which identity from the certificate to send, since only it knows why it is connecting. The recipient uses that identity first when selecting policy, and the most specific policy when wildcards overlap.
sections.plainLanguage: Before you talk, you say your name and show a card. The other side must check that the name you said really appears on the card, and only then decide what you are allowed to do.

sections.title: Certificate Requests and Certificates in IKEv1
sections.content:
A CERTREQ payload asks the peer for certificates; a CERT payload carries one. Only three certificate types matter here: X.509 Certificate - Signature, Revocation Lists (CRL and ARL), and PKCS #7 wrapped X.509 certificate. The last is deprecated.

In IKEv1 Main Mode, CERTREQ MUST appear in messages 4 and 5, and CERT in messages 5 and 6. An implementation that wants certificates in-band MUST send at least one CERTREQ, and one that sends none SHOULD NOT expect any CERT payloads.

CERTREQs SHOULD name the Certification Authority, using the Subject of each trust anchor local policy accepts. On receiving one, an implementation MUST send at least the end-entity certificate for that CA, unless policy says certificates are exchanged out of band. It MAY add intermediate CA certificates but SHOULD NOT send CRLs, ARLs or trust anchors, since that raises the chance of UDP fragmentation.

A CERTREQ with an empty Certification Authority field means "send all or any end-entity certificate you have". It exists for a gateway serving many peers with perhaps hundreds of trust anchors that cannot tell which one to name before it knows who the initiator is. Such a responder should first try to match the source IP in its policy database, then use configured default CAs, and only then send the empty form or terminate the negotiation with an error. If several end-entity certificates are sent, they MUST share the same public key.

Receivers MUST cope with unsupported certificate types, undecodable fields, unordered payloads, duplicates and irrelevant certificates. Optional optimizations let a peer hint at cached certificates by naming a lower CA, so that only the missing certificates are sent.
sections.plainLanguage: One side asks "show me an ID card from one of these offices", and the other shows the right card. If the asker does not know which offices to name, it can just say "show me any card you have".

sections.title: What Changes in IKEv2
sections.content:
For IKEv2, the Peer Authorization Database in RFC 4301 provides the formal model for binding identity to policy. IKEv2 adds an optional IDr payload, which the initiator may use to name which of the responder's identities to use. The initiator MUST be able to accept a responder-generated IDr of a different type.

In IKEv2 the CERTREQ payload must be in messages 2 and 3, and CERT in messages 3 and 4. The first CERT MUST contain an end-entity certificate that can authenticate the peer; the order of the others must not be assumed. One side may authenticate with certificates while the other uses pre-shared keys.

IKEv2 also defines a "Hash and URL of X.509 certificate" form, useful for devices with little memory and bandwidth. A sender that supports URL lookups can send the HTTP_CERT_LOOKUP_SUPPORTED notification. It then MUST support the http scheme, MAY support ftp, and MUST NOT require a specific form of the url-path. Like IKEv1, IKEv2 does not support certificate payloads over approximately 64K.
sections.plainLanguage: The newer version works the same way but does it in fewer steps. It also lets a small device say "just send me a web link to your card" instead of the whole card.

sections.title: The Certificate Profile
sections.content:
Implementations MUST conform to the PKIX certificate profile except where this document says otherwise. All checks MUST be enabled by default, though a configuration option to disable one may be offered for inflexible or noncompliant CAs. Version 3 certificates are required for everything except self-signed trust anchors.

CA software MUST be able to create Subjects with at least CN, C, O and OU. IKE implementations MUST accept an empty Subject, in which case identity is entirely in SubjectAltName. Distinguished names MUST NOT carry the emailAddress attribute.

  • KeyUsage: if present, digitalSignature or nonRepudiation MUST be set.
  • SubjectAltName: generate only rfc822Name, dNSName or iPAddress. No wildcards in dNSName and no CIDR notation in iPAddress.
  • BasicConstraints: CA certificates without it SHOULD be rejected by default.
  • ExtendedKeyUsage: a CA SHOULD NOT include it. The three IPsec-related values assigned in 1999 are deprecated. The RFC defines id-kp-ipsecIKE for the cases that need an EKU.
  • PrivateKeyUsagePeriod: CAs MUST NOT generate it.
  • CRLDistributionPoints and AuthorityInfoAccess: important, because revocation data is fetched out of band.
  • NameConstraints, PolicyConstraints, InhibitAnyPolicy: many implementations lack support, so CAs aiming for interoperability SHOULD NOT generate them.

Implementations may ignore the criticality bit of extensions they support but MUST honor it for extensions they do not support.
sections.plainLanguage: Not every fancy feature of a digital ID card is useful here, and many machines cannot read the fancy ones. So the rulebook lists which parts to include, which to skip, and which to refuse.

sections.title: Revocation and Signature Hashes
sections.content:
IKE implementations MUST use certificate revocation information when validating certificates, and SHOULD support CRLs unless a non-CRL method is the only one in use. Because sending CRLs inside IKE is deprecated, a certificate should point to its revocation data through CRLDistributionPoints (for CRLs) or AuthorityInfoAccess (for OCSP). Deployments need a URL in local configuration or in those extensions, and the pointers SHOULD be resolvable. Unresolvable ones such as http://localhost/path_to_CRL are as good as none.

If several trusted sources disagree, the conservative answer wins: one trusted report of revocation means the certificate MUST be considered revoked. Implementations MUST validate that CRLDistributionPoints matches IssuingDistributionPoint when the CA uses them, to prevent CRL substitution.

Delta CRLs are discouraged. Some implementations mishandle them, so the RFC RECOMMENDS NOT issuing them at this time, and implementations that do not support them MUST reject CRLs carrying the critical DeltaCRLIndicator and use a base CRL instead. Appendix A explains the risk: a naive algorithm fetches only the newest CRL, which may be a delta, and stops checking if that CRL fails to decode.

Implementations MUST be able to validate certificates signed with RSA-with-SHA1 and RSA-with-MD5, as popular CAs used them. Because both hashes are weaker than expected against collisions, implementations SHOULD also be able to use sha256WithRSAEncryption as soon as possible.
sections.plainLanguage: A lost or stolen ID card has to be cancelled, and checking the cancellation list should not slow down the handshake. So the card says where to look it up, and if any trusted list says "cancelled", the card is refused.

sections.title: Configuration Data Exchange Conventions
sections.content:
To move keying material between systems for configuration, implementations MUST support a common text format. They MUST accept arbitrary whitespace and line lengths and the line endings LF, CR and CRLF, and SHOULD generate lines of fewer than 76 characters. Data is Base64 encoded between delimiters.

  • Certificates: -----BEGIN CERTIFICATE----- and -----END CERTIFICATE-----
  • CRLs and ARLs: -----BEGIN CRL----- and -----END CRL-----
  • Raw public keys (the SubjectPublicKeyInfo part only): -----BEGIN PUBLIC KEY----- and -----END PUBLIC KEY-----
  • PKCS#10 signing requests: -----BEGIN CERTIFICATE REQUEST----- and -----END CERTIFICATE REQUEST-----

IKE implementations MUST support two forms of public keys: certificates and raw keys.
sections.plainLanguage: When people swap ID cards by copy and paste, they all wrap them in the same labeled envelope so any machine can tell what is inside.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
The contents of CERTREQ are not encrypted in IKE, which may leak private information in some environments. Using the empty Certification Authority option avoids this, at a cost in performance.

In IKEv1 Main Mode, certificates may be included in any message. Sending CERTs in messages 5 and 6 offers privacy protection, while sending them in the second message would violate Main Mode's identity protection.

Wherever the RFC suggests a configuration option to simplify, modify or disable a check, doing so may have security consequences. Such options MUST default to enabled, and warning users when they are disabled is appropriate. The RFC also notes that being unable to reach revocation data out of band is a potential vulnerability an attacker could exploit.
sections.plainLanguage: Some of the asking is done out loud where others can hear. Skipping safety checks might be needed sometimes, but the checks should always start switched on.
